newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU set to issue economic report in critical year.
newsitem.headline: EU set to issue economic report in critical year.

text.p: Against a backdrop of German unemployment at a 64-year high, the European Commission this week offers a sweeping annual review of the European Union economy in 1996 and an assessment of the challenges ahead.
Senior Commission officials late last week could not confirm the exact timing of the report, but last- minute adjustments were believed to have made Tuesday the most likely release date.
The current year is critical for countries wishing to qualify for a planned single European currency and the EU executive's yearly update is certain to be scrutinised more closely than usual.
Countries must bring their budget deficits and inflation rates in line with the Maastricht treaty this year if they hope to qualify for monetary union, expected to start in 1999.
Yet officials stressed that the 130-page document will not include any revised estimates for growth or budgetary performance during 1997 or 1998.
Fresh economic outlooks for all 15 nations will be forthcoming in the spring, incorporating the most recent data from late last year.
As a result, the Commission will reiterate its expectation of a 2.3 percent rise in the EU's gross domestic product this year and a further increase to 2.8 percent in 1998.
Regarding Germany, still Europe's main economic engine, officials said it was still too early to tell whether they will have to alter their estimates for 1997.

Two important influences are at work: the first is the dampening effects of a somewhat harsher winter and the second is the strong dollar, which at the margin should allow Germany more opportunities for export growth.
"We can't yet determine the outcome for Germany," one official said.
During its last round of forecasts in October, the Commission confidently predicted that Germany would bring its 1997 budget deficit down to three percent of GDP, the Maastricht treaty's requirement.

But weaker than expected growth in recent weeks combined with record joblessness have sown doubts among independent analysts on whether Bonn can meet the Maastricht target without further budget cuts.
The Commission's document will also highlight some of the key structural problems facing the EU, such as the competitive effects from an increasing integrated and globalised world economy.
There will also be an investigation into why budgetary restraint is needed apart from the preconditions of a common currency as well as a review of EU monetary policies.
